explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Amos says he sees a basket of summer fruit, and the LORD answers, "The end has come for My people Israel; I will no longer spare them." (Amos 8:2) Amos was just asked a simple question, and it turned into the heaviest answer of his day. I think that basket stopped looking so pretty to him right then.

I get why you'd lean that way, friend. A basket of summer fruit sounds like a gift on somebody's porch. But the LORD says, "The end has come for My people Israel; I will no longer spare them." (Amos 8:2) No blessing in that line.

A new king would at least come with a parade, friend. This word has no parade in it. The LORD tells Amos, "The end has come for My people Israel; I will no longer spare them." (Amos 8:2) Nobody is crowned there, and the word is about an ending.

Yes, wailing. The Lord GOD says, "the songs of the temple will turn to wailing." (Amos 8:3) The music doesn't just get quieter. It turns into something else completely. I think that's a sound nobody in that temple wanted to hear.
Whispers would almost be gentle, friend. But the Lord GOD doesn't say the songs fade out. He says they "will turn to wailing." (Amos 8:3) That's a loud, crying-out kind of sound, not a hush.
Cheering is the opposite direction, friend. The songs of the temple turn the other way, and the Lord GOD says they "will turn to wailing." (Amos 8:3) Nobody is throwing confetti in this verse.

Right on. They ask, "When will the New Moon be over, that we may sell grain?" (Amos 8:5) The New Moon and the Sabbath are in their way, and they're checking the clock. I'd call that a baker watching the timer, except this timer is counting down to cheating people.

explanations.answer: So they can go to war
explanations.explanation: War isn't in this verse, friend. These people want the New Moon and the Sabbath to end "that we may sell grain" and "market wheat." (Amos 8:5) Their eyes are on the market, not the battlefield.

Nobody's packing a suitcase here, friend. The question is, "When will the New Moon be over, that we may sell grain?" (Amos 8:5) The thing they're itching to get back to is business, and it's a crooked business.

True, friend. They say, "Let us reduce the ephah and increase the shekel; let us cheat with dishonest scales." (Amos 8:5) That's three tricks in one sentence. I'm impressed by the planning and ashamed of the purpose.

Not quite, friend. The text says they plan to do all of it together: "Let us reduce the ephah and increase the shekel; let us cheat with dishonest scales." (Amos 8:5) The dishonest scales are right there in the plan, so this one is true.

I wish it worked like that, friend, but no. The LORD says, "I will never forget any of their deeds." (Amos 8:7) Nothing fades with time here. He swears it by the Pride of Jacob, so the answer is False.
False is right, friend. The LORD has sworn by the Pride of Jacob: "I will never forget any of their deeds." (Amos 8:7) There's no "in time" in that sentence. He says never, and He swore it.

The Nile, friend. The land will "swell like the Nile; it will surge and then subside like the Nile in Egypt." (Amos 8:8) That river rises and falls, and the whole land is pictured doing the same. Big movement, no way to stand still.

The Jordan is a famous river, friend, so I see why it came to mind. But the text says the land will "swell like the Nile." (Amos 8:8) It names the Nile twice in that verse, so there's no mixing it up.
The Euphrates is a big river too, friend, but it isn't the one here. Amos 8:8 says the land will "surge and then subside like the Nile in Egypt." The Nile gets named twice in the same verse.

An only son, friend. The LORD says, "I will make it like a time of mourning for an only son, and its outcome like a bitter day." (Amos 8:10) That's about as deep as grief gets. I think this is a verse to read slowly.

A great king would be a big funeral, friend, but that isn't the picture. The LORD says, "I will make it like a time of mourning for an only son." (Amos 8:10) That's a grief that hits a family close to home.

An old friend is a sad loss, friend, but it isn't what the verse says. The LORD says, "I will make it like a time of mourning for an only son, and its outcome like a bitter day." (Amos 8:10) It's the mourning of a family losing their only son.

Words, friend. The Lord GOD says it will be "a famine of hearing the words of the LORD." (Amos 8:11) A full cupboard and a full glass won't help with that kind of hunger. Some hunger only God's words can feed.

Songs are close to the neighborhood, friend, since the passage already mentioned them in 8:3 and 8:10. But the famine is "a famine of hearing the words of the LORD." (Amos 8:11) It's about His words, not music.

Blessings sounds nice, friend, but it isn't the word here. The Lord GOD says, "not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the words of the LORD." (Amos 8:11) The thing missing is His words.

Hold on, friend, that's the part that gets me. The text says people will stagger and roam, "seeking the word of the LORD, but they will not find it." (Amos 8:12) They search hard and come up empty, so the answer is False.

False is right, friend. People will "stagger from sea to sea and roam from north to east, seeking the word of the LORD, but they will not find it." (Amos 8:12) All that searching, and the finding doesn't happen. That's a long walk with nothing at the end of it.

explanations.answer: They will fall, never to rise again
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. The LORD says of those who swear by Samaria's guilt, Dan's god and the way of Beersheba, "they will fall, never to rise again." (Amos 8:14) Swearing by those things didn't give them anything solid to stand on. The ending of this passage is a serious one.

explanations.answer: They will rise up and rule again
explanations.explanation: That's the reverse of what's written, friend. The LORD says, "they will fall, never to rise again." (Amos 8:14) The rising and ruling part isn't in the verse.

explanations.answer: They will run off to live in Egypt
explanations.explanation: No road trip in this verse, friend. The LORD says of them, "they will fall, never to rise again." (Amos 8:14) Egypt isn't mentioned in that line, and neither is any escape.
